title: The Fight Over Food for Peace: Feeding the Hungry or Helping Farmers?
summary:
Imagine a program that has fed 4 billion hungry people in 150 countries over 70 years. That's Food for Peace! It was started by a Kansas farmer in the 1950s to send American grain to people who don't have enough to eat. But this year, it almost disappeared.

When President Trump took office, he stopped all foreign aid. The agency that ran Food for Peace, called USAID, was shut down. Suddenly, food shipments to millions of starving people stopped. Farmers like Merrill Nielsen in Kansas were also hurt. He said the program helps him sell crops he otherwise couldn't, and without it, prices dropped.

Farm-state lawmakers quickly worked to bring the program back, but they moved it to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). USDA knows how to buy food—it's spending $450 million on American grain to ship overseas. But critics say USDA doesn't know how to deliver food aid to the people who need it most.

Dina Esposito, who led Food for Peace for six years, says USDA has no humanitarian experts. She says it's bypassing the worst hunger crises, like Sudan, where 21 million people face starvation. USDA says it focuses on places where it can deliver food safely and monitor it well. It also promises to use mostly American ships and food, which is great for U.S. farmers and shipping companies.

But Esposito says that makes the program less efficient, so fewer hungry people get help. "That assistance is the difference between life and death for that child," she said.

Now, Congress is deciding the program's future. The House wants to keep it at USDA permanently. The Senate hasn't agreed yet. Supporters say USDA needs a couple of years to prove it can do the job. If not, a program that's been a lifeline for billions could end forever.
why_it_matters: When you eat a meal, think about how decisions by leaders can affect whether a child on the other side of the world gets to eat too—it shows how connected we all are.

background_read: Food aid programs like Food for Peace started after World War II to help countries that had trouble growing enough food.
The U.S. government created USAID in 1961 to handle foreign aid, including food, medicine, and disaster relief.
Recently, the U.S. stopped many aid programs to save money, which raised debates about what should come first—helping American farmers or feeding starving families in other countries.

WHAT: The Food for Peace program was moved from USAID to the USDA after USAID was shut down.
WHERE: The help goes from the U.S. to hungry people in many countries, like Sudan.
WHY: President Trump stopped foreign aid, so Congress saved the program by putting it under USDA, but now there are arguments about whether that works.
